issues.legal_issue: A prior constitutional judgment does not operate as res judicata when the later claim arises from a distinct interference under a subsequently enacted law.
material_facts: An earlier judgment had restrained interference with the firm's contractual right to collect forest produce insofar as the interference was based on the abolition legislation.
The later interference was based on a statute enacted after that judgment to regulate trade in tendu leaves.
The earlier judgment did not expressly decide that the firm's contract itself was a property right, and subsequent decisions had treated the earlier judgment as given per incuriam on that point.
issues.conclusion: The earlier judgment did not operate as res judicata because the causes of action were distinct and the later law created circumstances not considered in the earlier proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: Res judicata does not apply where the later proceeding concerns a distinct cause of action arising under a new law that alters the circumstances addressed in the earlier proceeding. The Court treated Chhotabhai Jethabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh as no longer binding as a precedent on the property-right point, relying on Shantabai v. State of Bombay and Mahadeo v. State of Bombay. It considered Hoystead v. Commissioner of Taxation but found it did not govern the distinct cause of action, and noted Society of Medical Officers of Health v. Hope and Broken Hill Proprietary Company Limited v. Municipal Council of Broken Hill in discussing the limits of Hoystead.

predicates.constitutional_writ_petition: The claimant brings a constitutional writ proceeding relying on a judgment in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.prior_judgment_concerned_different_inter: The earlier proceeding concerned interference with the claimant's asserted rights under a different legal measure.
predicates.current_interference_arises_under_later_: The present interference is said to arise under a law enacted after the earlier judgment.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ claim concerns a later interference under a later law, and the earlier judgment concerned a different interference, that judgment does not bar the current claim.

issues.legal_issue: A contractual right to collect natural produce does not constitute a property right in produce that remains attached to the land.
material_facts: The firm held an agreement granting it a right to pluck and carry tendu leaves from specified villages for a fixed term.
The agreement gave the firm no interest in the land or the trees themselves.
When the later law interfered with the firm's asserted right, the relevant leaves had not yet been plucked.
The firm sought to enforce the asserted right through a constitutional petition alleging an invasion of property.
issues.conclusion: The firm had only a contractual right, not a property right in leaves before they were plucked, and therefore could not invoke constitutional protection of property on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Article 32 provides a remedy for enforcement of fundamental rights, but a right to contract is not itself a right to property. A claimant who has only a contractual collection right has no property in natural produce before it is severed. The Court relied on Shantabai v. State of Bombay and Mahadeo v. State of Bombay, and explained why Chhotabhai Jethabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh could not establish the contrary proposition; it also referred to Article 19(1)(f) in describing the earlier claims.

predicates.constitutional_property_claim: The claimant seeks constitutional relief on the basis that an asserted right to collect natural produce is a property right.
predicates.claimant_has_only_contractual_collection: The claimant's asserted entitlement to collect the produce arises only from a contract and gives no interest in the land or the holding.
predicates.leaves_remain_attached_when_right_is_inv: The produce that the claimant seeks to collect remains attached to the land when the asserted right is interfered with.
predicates.claimant_has_no_interest_in_holding: The claimant has no independent interest in the holding on which the produce grows.

issues.definition: A constitutional property claim does not establish a property right in produce where the claimant has only a contractual collection right, no interest in the holding, and the produce remains attached.

issues.legal_issue: A valid later law may regulate or displace contractual collection rights despite an earlier judgment, without expressly stating that it overrides that judgment.
material_facts: The later statute restricted the purchase and transport of tendu leaves to the State, its authorised officers, or its agents, subject to specified exceptions.
A person without an interest in the holding who had acquired a right to collect leaves was treated under the statute as having purchased them in contravention of its provisions.
The firm's entitlement arose from a contract with the former proprietor, and the firm was not a grower or a person with an interest in the holding.
The earlier judgment had addressed the effect of the abolition legislation, not the later trade-regulation statute.
The later statute was not challenged as invalid.
issues.conclusion: The later statute applied to the firm and its contractual rights were no longer available; it had to obtain leaves through the statutory system like any other person.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Tendu Patta (Vyapar Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1964 restricted purchase and transport to the State, authorised officers, and agents; Explanation I addressed purchases from those authorised sellers, Explanation II treated a non-holder's acquired collection right as a prohibited purchase, and subsections (2) and (3) regulated permitted transport and sale. A later law that creates circumstances rendering an earlier decision inapplicable may have that effect without an express clause beginning 'notwithstanding anything contained in a judgment'. The earlier decision concerned the Abolition Act and did not determine the effect of the later Adhiniyam; the Court stated that the Legislature could enact a valid law affecting the claimant's asserted rights, and the law was not challenged as invalid.

rule.if: challenge_to_later_trade_regulation and later_law_changes_legal_circumstances and state_monopoly_law_restricts_purchase_and_transport and claimant_relies_on_prior_contract and prior_judgment_concerned_different_law and law_not_challenged_as_invalid

predicates.challenge_to_later_trade_regulation: The claimant brings a proceeding challenging the effect of a later law regulating trade in the natural produce.
predicates.later_law_changes_legal_circumstances: The later law creates legal circumstances that were not present when the earlier judgment was given.
predicates.state_monopoly_law_restricts_purchase_an: The later law reserves or restricts the purchase and transport of the produce through a state-controlled system.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_prior_contract: The claimant asserts that a pre-existing contract entitles it to collect or acquire the produce despite the later law.
predicates.prior_judgment_concerned_different_law: The earlier judgment addressed interference under a different law rather than the later trade-regulation law.
predicates.law_not_challenged_as_invalid: The claimant does not challenge the later law as invalid.

issues.definition: When a claimant relies on a prior contract and judgment to avoid a valid, later state-controlled trade system that changes the legal circumstances, the later law applies to the claimant.
